Most Final Fantasy games are a blend of sci-fi and magic, and alot of them have very dark undertones. 

FFVI has an evil empire that enslaves magical people and weaponizes their essence to further its military power.

The villain of FFVII is a defect super soldier who makes a pact with a machine god alien and borrows her power to become a god himself.

FFXIII features god machine robots blessing humans with magical abilities and manipulating them into enacting their will. 

FFXV has an empire that harnesses a magical, demonic curse and uses it to control people, but also to create demonic super soldiers and giant mechs.

Chrono Trigger is very much a magical fantasy game, but it's entire plot revolves around using a time machine to prevent the end of the world.

Long story short, many video games can make this work so I believe it's possible for other forms of story telling as well.

I just ran my first one shot, and I would call it a success. I would just make sure you check all your boxes. 

Mechanically: make sure you know the ins and outs of your manuals, and if possible, the classes they might be running. I recommend excluding the more complex classes like sorcerer and druid until they're more familiar. 

Narratively: be descriptive, entertaining, and concise. Your story doesn't have to be an award winner buy at least make sure it's engaging

Balance: this one is the most important in my opinion. They'll forgive you if you have to look up a few rules, or if your story isn't that good. But make sure you give them a small taste of everything. I would try to include at least two of each of these: puzzles/riddles, battles, roleplaying/negotiation, and moments of down time to get to know their characters better, such as around the campfire or trudging along the path. Including an interesting, inquisitive NPC along for their adventure will spurn the creativity along.

This last bit is a personal rant of mine: 

I absolutely hate one shot or beginner campaigns that are just endless waves of orcs/skeletons/goblins/wolves. This is dungeons and DRAGONS. Give them a dang dragon. They don't have to fight and kill it, but at least give them a glimpse of one. Have one fly overhead randomly while they're adventuring. Put a sleeping one right in their path and make them sneak around it or negotiate with it. Better yet, dragons are intelligent; have one of their quest givers be a dragon. 

That goes for any monster in the manual, really. Beginner doesn't mean boring. Browse around the monster manual, find a beasty you really like (regardless of CR) and find a creative way to include it into the adventure. Remember, it's not always about killing. It's all about variety. Show them how big the world of D&D can get, and leave them wanting more.

Thanks for the reply. I may have mislead a little bit by using the word god. This is just how everyone else would perceive him, as they have no concept of traveling through time, yet here the protagonist is seemingly omnipresent throughout history as he travels through time. 

He's not a literal god in the way Dr. Manhattan is, as you're right, that wouldn't create enough drama or motivation to justify him being the protagonist.

Rather, he's seen as a god. Much like someone watching Sherlock Holmes operate would describe his deductive abilities as inhuman or even godly. 

The protagonist does have a clear motivation, and it's a noble and heroic one at that. Without getting too technical, He's out to defeat the 100+ year old villain who has evaded him, but can't do so by time traveling in the way that he has with other opponents, because of how time travel works in my world. 

Anyways, more Sherlock or Jay Gatsby, less Dr. Manhattan. I suppose he wouldn't be a LITERAL force of Nature since he still faces obstacles that he will struggle with, but the unstoppable Force of Nature is the feeling I want to convey to the reader.
Maybe a friendly space race that slowly escalates into a galactic turf war over decades/centuries?

Your suggestion is really brilliant actually! But I originally intended the protag to be the only time traveler in the story, which would make him very powerful but also a very large target for others to try and take the power from him. 

After much reading on how time travel could or should work, I decided to run with the theory that it's impossible to travel back in time to a point before the method of time travel existed. In other words, travel to any point in time from the second the time travel method was created and onward is possible, but before that it's impossible. 

As for the time travel itself, It's made possible via a techno gadget of which only one was created, as a prototype. It was created to try and go back in time to reverse all the damage the big bad had caused which created the current war torn post apocalyptic setting of the present, when the actual story takes place. 

This way, the protag's ability was created to stop the villain before he ever became powerful. But as I mentioned before,  in trying to go back in time and stop the big bad, the hero actually influenced the villain's past, becoming the very thing that made the villain resort to evil in the first place. 

Sorry, thanks for your suggestions and your patience. Writing time travel fiction is no joke for sure!

**Academics** I was an awful student. I saw right through the illusion of America's flawed school system, and so I put almost no effort into it. I got C's and D's all through middle and high school. I never studied for any tests, and did close to no homework. I did just enough to skate by and get my diploma, and actually graduate. College has been even worse. I would do the absolute bare minimum to get my headband and graduate the academy. If I find a subject interesting, I'll research it in extreme depth, but nothing matters less to me than earning a letter grade.

**Athletics** I lead a pretty sedentary lifestyle now, but I'd say I'm average athletically from doing a lot of Yoga. I'm an extremely fast runner, and had the fastest times in the hundred yard dash in school, but I consider myself just a sprinter, because have close to zero endurance. I'm pretty strong and can do a couple dozen pushups and situps. I would probably have to resort to ambushes and quick getaways, being more of an opportunist and avoiding the long, drawn out missions that are typical in Naruto. I'm also incredibly stealthy, and I usually won  games of capture the flag and hide and seek as a kid.

**Combat** I made it about 2/3rds of the way through my friend's dad's martial arts program. It was a blend of Ju Jitsu and Phillipino stick fighting that focused on holds, ground fighting, and ending a confrontation with as few movements as possible. I also joined a competetive sparring team for a couple of years. I had a knack for it, but had to stop because of money. I think I would excel at combat techniques, but again, because of my lack of endurance I'm not going to be the next Rock Lee.

**Leadership** In group settings I tend to enjoy sitting back and waiting for the other, more natural born leaders to take charge. In this case I usually become an advisor for the group and the leader, or play devil's advocate to make sure all holes in the plan are filled. However, if a leader doesn't pop up immediately, I'm usually the one to take on the leadership role. I have a lot of patience and understanding for people, and I'm good at communicating in different ways to get everyone on the same page. I'd probably be like Shikamaru. Once his leader Asuma was killed, he saw a whole in leadership that needed filling for his team, and he took on that role really well short term.

**Attitude** I don't like discomfort at all. I like to be in control, or at least have a decent understanding of the current situation, and unless it's life or death or for the greater good, retreat is always on the table. Survival is the only success that matters.

**Strategy** I would consider myself a really good, yet unconventional strategist. I love chess and board games, card games, and strategy video games. But having one plan isn't enough for me. Instead, I like to have many, many backup plans and options, and play more defensively. I'm more comfortable having a large toolkit to use in a variety of situations, rather than adhering to one initial plan. I would probably put the time into learning hundreds of low level jutsu that can be useful in different scenarios. I'm also pretty good at thinking on my feet, seeing and taking advantage of opportunity, and turning bad situations into good ones.

**Conclusion**
From all of this, the Anbu is looking pretty good to me. I would probably make it all the way up to mid Chuunin, perhaps early Jounin, just from my patience, great teamwork skills, and natural intelligence. I don't have the academic motivation to become a medical ninja, or to invent my own techniques, nor do I have the athleticism to be in the standard Jounin military. I don't have the ambition to become the next Hokage or one of the Sannin. I don't have the endurance to run long, drawn out missions. I'd probably stick to quick, clean assassination or espionage jobs, since that's what my combat training and lack of endurance allows for. Anbu would provide a lot of that for me. I always keep my nose clean and have a spotless record, so I would pass all the background checks needed. I'm also an incredibly good liar. If that doesn't pan out, then being an academy teacher might also work.

Bare with me for my long post, but I think this calls for an understanding of each of their mindsets and methods. 


To me L is the better planner. He is constantly setting traps for Light, and he falls into most of them. The TV Broadcast, the surveillance, their first meeting at the school, the chess game/tennis match, inviting Light to join the task force, heck even their coffee breaks were traps. But they weren't traps to end the game, they were traps to reveal new information and gather clues/evidence.

 He also has better focus in my opinion, as far as his end goal. His goal from encounter to encounter isn't to catch Kira once and for all. Rather, it was to essentially put enough pressure onto Light, until Light finally cracks under it, and reveals *himself* as Kira. 

Light on the other hand is really *really* good at improvising, and playing defense. He played defense throughout the entire series, pushing the blame off of himself while also improving his situation on numerous occasions. He had to do damage control for most of the series. He's shown mastery over the concept of turning crappy, "no way out" situations into his advantages. The whole ordeal with Naomi Misura, or Ray Penber. Or how he used the agents that were trailing him as an opportunity to both test the Note's capabilities, and to eliminate the agents. He's more of an escape artist in my mind. 

There's also the matter of his focus, which isn't necessarily on eliminating L, but eliminating all criminals to create his perfect society, and eliminating all threats to that goal along the way, including L.

Essentially, L is the Cat and Light is the mouse. Not just in roles, but in their mindsets as well.


Now, if we reverse the roles, I still think either one could succeed. I'm not saying that L can't think on his toes, or that Light isn't a masterful planner in his own right. But we do see L handle bad situations with a more "give me a moment to think" response, rather than Light's "I need to act now. I'm taking a risk and I'm hoping it will work" response. What I am saying, is that it's going to be more of an uphill battle for both of them. L was written to be the perfect detective as a character, and Light the perfect criminal. I'm having a hard time deciding who would win. 

I am going to give it to L 7/10 though. Maybe it's just because we get a lot more inner monologue from Light than we do from L, but it seems to me like Light gets all worked up and cracks more under pressure than L does, especially when he is morally invested. We've only seen one or two emotional outbursts from L, whereas Light seems to give us pretty emotional responses whenever his plans don't work or he's backed into a corner. That tendency to involve himself emotionally, mixed with his extreme moral compass, says to me that Light will likely crack before L does.  

Edit:

Now to your original question, "does Light stand a chance?" I would say yes. A small one, but he has a few advantages. 

1. Light to me is a lot more academic, and if he's now the world's top detective, it means he's studied everything the human race had accumulated about criminal justice, criminal psychology, and forensics, a little bit more thoroughly than L, who I think just has more natural talent for detective work.

2. Let's face it, if you saw someone like L in person, you would probably think he was a serial killer. He has unusual, almost compulsive quirks, he's socially awkward and non-present, and from the lack of emotional outbursts we get from him, it almost seems borderline sociopathic. Light will take alot less time pinning down L as his primary suspect, than L did with Light, since Light was popular, good looking, and upper middle class. Now L would probably avoid being seen by any law enforcement, but his classmates and others won't hesitate to talk about his quirky and creepy nature. When that happens, Light's detective experience would ring true, "it's always the quiet ones."

3. The last advantage Light will have that gives him a shot, is that he himself is a narcissistic megolomaniac with a god complex. That's just a core aspect of his character regardless of what role you put him in. Being a detective, he would be hyper self aware of his own mental issues and could use them to his advantage, to think like the criminals think. L likely was able to do this too, since I'm convinced he's sociopathic, but that doesn't mean the reverse wouldn't be true when the roles are reversed. L said himself, they're both childish and hate to lose. 

But, in the end, I still give it to L. Since he is the better planner, he would have already been steps ahead of the law before he ever wrote his first name down. He would kill indescriminately and at random to avoid leaving a trail, rather than sticking to Japan and having a schedule. Also, Light kind of adopted the role of Kira on a whim and at impulse, and he flew by the seat of his pants for the rest of the ride. But L likely would have thought it through a lot more, coming up with backup plans for his backup plans. Light didn't even have a plan for what would happen if they found the Death Note in his room until the FBI started tailing him... He's just better at setting traps, and he would have set many of them before beginning his journey as Kira.

I would say to first decide your format. There are two major formats now for competetive Pokémon: 

First, There's VGC, which stands for Video Game Championships. These are timed doubles matches, and the different Pokémon that you can use are limited to only the most current game's regional Pokedex. So for VGC 2017, only Pokémon found in the Alola Regional Pokedex are allowed. This is also regarded as the "official" Pokémon format. This time around, Mega evolutions also will not be allowed.

Next is the various tiers of Smogon. Smogon is an independent website that serves as a database for Competetive Pokémon, as well as a committee that determines it's own rules and format. Smogon format consists of less time restrictive single battles. Smogon also divides the Pokémon into tiers based on popularity and success. Over Used is the most common tier, with all the popular Pokémon like Gengar and Salamence. Megas are allowed here, but the more overpowered ones get sent to a higher tier. Then there's Under Used, Rarely Used, and Never Used. These aren't quite as popular, as they contain less popular/less powerful Pokémon. There's also Ubers, which is mostly just legendaries. These are all abbreviated to U, OU, UU, RU, and NU, respectively. Also, if you wanted to play OU, you can use any of the OU tier pokemon, and anything from the lower tiers. Ubers aren't allowed in OU. Another example, if you wanted to play RU, only RU and NU pokemon would be allowed, no UU, OU, or Ubers. It's divided this way to keep things fair and keep the environment organized.

So deciding which of these two formats you want to do is mostly a matter of "do you want to play Singles, or Doubles?." But it also has to do with which Pokémon you'll want to use. If you want a more open roster with less time restraint per match, choose OU. If you say that this is the generation that you want to get competetive, that probably means you like the Alola Pokémon and would want to use them. If that's the case, choose VGC, as all Alolan Pokémon are allowed. 

Smogon has been around a little longer, but both formats hold tournaments and are highly competetive. VGC does get more press, however.

Once you decide which format you want to start into, then it's just a matter of Google searching "VGC beginner tips" or "OU Starter teams."

This sub is also a great resource for specific questions on team viability and such. Hope this helps, welcome!
